items.html: Non-high-density cholesterol. It is total cholesterol minus high-density cholesterol, and in hypertriglyceridemia it assesses heart-disease risk better than low-density lipoprotein alone.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 116

src.question: How is non-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol calculated?
src.explanation: Non-high-density cholesterol is total cholesterol minus high-density cholesterol, and in hypertriglyceridemia it assesses heart-disease risk better than low-density lipoprotein alone.

items.html: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia. An apolipoprotein E mutation, associated with apolipoprotein E2 homozygosity, lets chylomicron and very-low-density remnants accumulate, so triglyceride and total cholesterol both rise to 250 to 500 mg/dL.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 55

src.question: What causes the lipid elevation in familial dysbetalipoproteinemia?
src.key: Accumulation of chylomicron and very-low-density remnants
src.explanation: An apolipoprotein E mutation, associated with apolipoprotein E2 homozygosity, lets chylomicron and very-low-density remnants accumulate, so triglyceride and total cholesterol both rise to 250 to 500 mg/dL.

items.html: Risk-enhancing factors favoring a statin. These include persistent triglyceride of 175 mg/dL or more, family history of premature disease, persistent low-density lipoprotein of 160 or more, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease and South Asian ancestry.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 105

src.question: Which is a risk-enhancing factor that favors statin therapy?
src.explanation: Risk enhancers include persistent triglyceride of 175 mg/dL or more, family history of premature disease, persistent low-density lipoprotein of 160 or more, metabolic syndrome, chronic kidney disease and South Asian ancestry.

items.html: Severe hypertriglyceridemia. The pattern is triglyceride above 500 mg/dL with elevated total cholesterol and reduced high-density lipoprotein, usually without elevated low-density lipoprotein or apolipoprotein B.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 43

src.question: Which lipid pattern is typical of severe hypertriglyceridemia?
src.key: High triglyceride, low high-density, normal low-density
src.explanation: Triglyceride above 500 mg/dL with elevated total cholesterol and reduced high-density lipoprotein, usually without elevated low-density lipoprotein or apolipoprotein B.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Secondary causes, and what to rule out before a statin
items.html: Estrogen and lipids. Estrogen can elevate triglyceride (while increasing high-density lipoprotein), so patients starting birth control pills or postmenopausal estrogen, or who are pregnant, are monitored.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 62

src.question: A 26-year-old woman with a borderline triglyceride of 170 mg/dL is starting a combined birth control pill. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
src.explanation: Estrogen can elevate triglyceride (while increasing high-density lipoprotein), so patients starting birth control pills or postmenopausal estrogen, or who are pregnant, are monitored.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Secondary causes, and what to rule out before a statin
items.html: Dietary carbohydrate and triglyceride. Excess carbohydrate increases hepatic very-low-density triglyceride secretion, raising triglyceride, so cutting it addresses a secondary cause.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 59

src.question: A 35-year-old man with a triglyceride of 250 mg/dL drinks several sugary sodas and eats white bread and pasta at every meal. Which dietary counseling point addresses a cause of his triglyceride?
src.explanation: Excess carbohydrate increases hepatic very-low-density triglyceride secretion, raising triglyceride, so reducing it addresses a secondary cause.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Secondary causes, and what to rule out before a statin
items.html: Anabolic steroids and lipids. Anabolic steroids decrease high-density lipoprotein, so they are a secondary cause of a low level, and stopping them addresses it.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 62

src.question: A 34-year-old bodybuilder has a high-density lipoprotein of 22 mg/dL. He admits to using anabolic steroids for two years. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
src.key: The steroids are lowering his good cholesterol
src.explanation: Anabolic steroids decrease high-density lipoprotein, so they are a secondary cause of his low level that stopping them addresses.

items.html: Weight goal in dyslipidemia. Therapeutic lifestyle changes aim for a 5% to 10% reduction of initial weight; for 200 pounds that is 10 to 20 pounds.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 75

src.question: A 54-year-old woman with dyslipidemia weighs 200 pounds and asks how much weight she should aim to lose. Which goal is most appropriate?
src.explanation: Therapeutic lifestyle changes aim for a 5% to 10% reduction of initial weight; for 200 pounds that is 10 to 20 pounds.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Secondary causes, and what to rule out before a statin
items.html: Thyroid testing before a statin. Decreased thyroid hormone down-regulates hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptors and raises low-density lipoprotein, so elevated levels call for screening for low thyroid before a statin.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 61

src.question: A 50-year-old man has low-density lipoprotein of 178 mg/dL. He reports fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance over the past year. Before a statin is started, which test should be ordered?
src.explanation: Decreased thyroid hormone down-regulates hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptors and raises low-density lipoprotein, so elevated levels call for screening for low thyroid before a statin.

items.html: Statins at ages 20 to 39. Lifetime risk is estimated to encourage lifestyle, and a statin is considered with a family history of premature disease and low-density lipoprotein of 160 or more.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 96

src.question: A 30-year-old man has low-density lipoprotein of 175 mg/dL. His father had a heart attack at 50, and he has no other risk factors. When should a statin be considered for him?
src.key: Now, given family history and his level
src.explanation: At 20 to 39, lifetime risk is estimated to encourage lifestyle, and a statin is considered with a family history of premature disease and low-density lipoprotein of 160 or more.

items.html: Calcium score and statins. A coronary artery calcium score of 100 or more (or at or above the 75th percentile) indicates statin therapy unless the clinician-patient risk discussion defers it.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 106

src.question: A 58-year-old man without diabetes has a 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 9%. Because the statin decision was uncertain, a coronary artery calcium score was obtained, and it is 180. What is the most appropriate management?
src.explanation: A calcium score of 100 or more (or at or above the 75th percentile) indicates statin therapy unless the clinician-patient risk discussion defers it.

items.html: Xanthelasmas. They usually indicate an underlying genetic condition, and ruling out primary causes matters because they influence the patient's own risk and the management of family members.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 35

src.question: A 30-year-old woman has soft yellow plaques on both upper eyelids near the inner canthi (xanthelasmas). Her low-density lipoprotein is 205 mg/dL. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
src.key: They suggest an inherited lipid disorder
src.explanation: Xanthelasmas usually indicate an underlying genetic condition, and ruling out primary causes matters because they influence her own risk and the management of her family members.

items.html: Furosemide monitoring. Furosemide is a potassium-wasting loop diuretic, so potassium and renal function are followed on the complete metabolic panel.

src.question: A 70-year-old man with heart failure and congestion is started on furosemide. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
src.key: Potassium and kidney labs will be checked
src.explanation: Furosemide is a potassium-wasting loop diuretic, so potassium and renal function are followed on the complete metabolic panel.

items.section_title: 2.4 · Neurogenic vs non-neurogenic: the heart rate response
items.html: Heart rate response in orthostatic hypotension. A pressure fall with only a minimal heart rate rise means the sympathetic reflex is not compensating, which favors neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

src.question: A 66-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes fainted after walking to the bathroom. Supine she is 146/84 with a heart rate of 70; after 3 minutes standing she is 118/70 with a heart rate of 72. What does her heart rate response indicate?
src.explanation: A pressure fall with only a minimal heart rate rise means the sympathetic reflex is not compensating, which favors neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Treatment: remove the cause, educate, match the drug
items.html: Adherence in orthostatic hypotension. Understanding is the key to compliance: once a patient knows why the pressure falls on standing, slow position changes make sense and are followed.

src.question: A 70-year-old man with orthostatic hypotension keeps standing up quickly despite being told not to, because he does not see why it matters. Which approach most improves his adherence?
src.explanation: Understanding is the key to compliance: once a patient knows why the pressure falls on standing, slow position changes make sense and are followed.

items.html: Calcium channel blockers in heart failure. Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker, and calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure; pressure control comes from optimizing the recommended classes as tolerated.

src.question: A 69-year-old woman with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 27%) has blood pressure above goal on her heart failure regimen. Verapamil is proposed. What is the most appropriate response?
src.key: Avoid it and use recommended classes
src.explanation: Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker, and calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. Pressure control comes from optimizing the recommended classes as tolerated.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Treatment: remove the cause, educate, match the drug
items.html: Iatrogenic orthostatic hypotension. The offending agent is removed first: it is treated by reducing or removing the medication, with slow position changes meanwhile.

src.question: A 71-year-old man had his diuretic dose increased 10 days ago. He now has lightheadedness on standing, a 28 mmHg systolic fall and a heart rate rise from 70 to 94. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
src.explanation: The offending agent is removed first: iatrogenic hypotension is treated by reducing or removing the medication, with slow position changes meanwhile.

items.html: Hypertensive retinopathy. Blood pressure control can lead to regression of the retinopathy, so it is both a prognostic marker and something that can improve with treatment. It predicts long-term stroke risk independently of the pressure level.

src.question: A 55-year-old man with hypertensive retinopathy achieves good blood pressure control. What can be expected of his retinal findings?
src.key: Control can lead to regression of the retinopathy
src.explanation: so the finding is both a prognostic marker and something that can improve with treatment. Retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk independently of the pressure level.

items.html: Chronic kidney disease in hypertension. Not all of it is hypertensive, and diabetes must be evaluated; the relationship is bidirectional, so the presence of both does not establish which came first.

src.question: A 63-year-old with long-standing hypertension has an estimated filtration rate that has fallen over eighteen months and a rising urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. He also has type 2 diabetes. What should be done next?
src.key: Evaluate for alternative renal causes too
src.explanation: Not all chronic kidney disease in a hypertensive patient is hypertensive, and diabetes must be evaluated. The relationship is bidirectional, so the presence of both does not establish which came first.

items.html: Symptom log in reflex syncope. A log of pattern and frequency supports a history-based diagnosis of reflex syncope and helps identify the triggers to avoid.

src.question: A 27-year-old woman reports several brief faints over 6 months with a warm, nauseated prodrome, but she cannot recall what was happening before most of them. Her examination is normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Keep a log of each episode
src.explanation: A log of pattern and frequency supports a history-based diagnosis of reflex syncope and helps identify the triggers to avoid.

items.html: High-output heart failure treatment. It is treated by correcting the underlying cause of increased demand, such as hyperthyroidism, with a diuretic for congestion.

src.question: A 46-year-old woman with high-output heart failure from untreated hyperthyroidism has leg edema and breathlessness. Which treatment approach is most appropriate?
src.key: Treat the thyroid disease and add a diuretic
src.explanation: High-output failure is treated by correcting the underlying cause of increased demand, here hyperthyroidism, with a diuretic for congestion.

items.html: Family history as a coronary risk factor. It counts when a male first-degree relative had sudden death or myocardial infarction before 55, or a female first-degree relative before 65.

src.question: A 40-year-old woman's mother had a myocardial infarction at 70 and her brother had one at 50. She asks which relative's heart attack raises her own coronary risk. Which answer is accurate?
src.explanation: Family history counts when a male first-degree relative had sudden death or myocardial infarction before 55, or a female first-degree relative before 65. Her brother at 50 qualifies; her mother at 70 does not.

items.section_title: 2.9 · Treatment: remove the cause, educate, match the drug
items.html: Vasopressors. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.

src.question: A 70-year-old woman with non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from volume loss is lightheaded on standing in the clinic but alert, with a standing pressure of 100/62. Which treatment is inappropriate in this setting?
src.explanation: Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.

also.explanation: Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.
Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.

items.html: Titrating therapy in reduced ejection fraction. Guideline-directed therapy is prioritized for the patient's comorbidities and optimized as hemodynamically stable, so each class is increased as blood pressure and tolerance allow.

src.question: A 61-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction asks why his clinician raises one medicine at a time rather than starting everything at full strength. Which explanation is accurate?
src.explanation: Guideline-directed therapy is prioritized for his comorbidities and optimized as hemodynamically stable, so each class is increased as blood pressure and tolerance allow.

also.explanation: Therapy in reduced ejection fraction is prioritized for the patient's comorbidities and optimized as hemodynamically stable, meaning each class is increased as blood pressure and tolerance allow.

items.section_title: 5.9 · ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
items.html: Nitroglycerin in right ventricular infarction. Nitroglycerin reduces preload, removing the Frank-Starling effect the injured right ventricle depends on; output drops further, the right ventricle fails and shock follows.

src.question: A 68-year-old woman with right ventricular infarction (ST elevation in V4R) is given sublingual nitroglycerin in triage, and her blood pressure falls to 70/40 mmHg. What explains the fall?
src.explanation: Nitroglycerin reduces preload, which removes the Frank-Starling effect the injured right ventricle depends on. Output drops further, the right ventricle fails and the patient goes into shock.

items.html: Vasospastic angina timing. Pain most often occurs from midnight to early morning, more often between midnight and 8 in the morning, at rest, coming on and off gradually over 5 to 15 minutes.

src.question: When do vasospastic angina episodes most often occur?
src.explanation: Most patients with vasospastic angina have pain from midnight to early morning, more often between midnight and 8 in the morning, at rest, coming on and off gradually over 5 to 15 minutes.

items.html: Carvallo sign. Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so the tricuspid regurgitation murmur grows louder while mitral regurgitation does not; deep inspiration distinguishes them.

src.question: A 67-year-old woman has a holosystolic murmur, and the examiner is unsure whether it is tricuspid or mitral in origin. Which bedside maneuver best separates the two?
src.explanation: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so the tricuspid regurgitation murmur grows louder (the Carvallo sign) while mitral regurgitation does not. That distinguishes them.

items.html: Heart failure prevention at stage A. An at-risk patient with diabetes and a normal heart is stage A, where the first recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin. A beta blocker enters at stage B.

src.question: A 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a normal echocardiogram asks whether she should take metoprolol, as her father did, to prevent heart failure. Which reply is most accurate?
src.key: Dapagliflozin comes first, not a beta blocker
src.explanation: As an at-risk patient with diabetes and a normal heart she is stage A, where the first recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin. A beta blocker enters at stage B.

items.html: Modifiable heart failure risk factors. Tobacco, excessive alcohol and obesity are modifiable, whereas family history cannot be changed, so counseling targets the modifiable ones.

src.question: A 45-year-old woman with a family history of heart failure smokes, drinks heavily and is obese. Her heart is structurally normal. Which counseling point best lowers her heart failure risk?
src.key: Quit tobacco, cut alcohol, lose weight
src.explanation: Tobacco, excessive alcohol and obesity are modifiable risk factors for heart failure. Her family history is a risk factor she cannot change, so counseling targets the ones she can.

items.html: Apheresis. It is like dialysis: the elective removal of low-density particles from the circulation, and it is the treatment of choice for homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 109

src.question: A 7-year-old boy with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and under 2% of normal receptor activity asks, through his parents, why he needs frequent sessions attached to a machine. Which explanation is most appropriate?
src.key: It filters the bad cholesterol out
src.explanation: Apheresis is like dialysis: the elective removal of low-density particles from the circulation, and it is the treatment of choice for the homozygous disorder.

items.section_title: 5.11 · After the infarct: complications, secondary prevention, sudden cardiac death
items.html: Diltiazem after myocardial infarction. Diltiazem and verapamil do not lower mortality; when a beta blocker cannot be used they relieve angina or control rate, provided function is preserved and there is no heart failure.

src.question: A 63-year-old woman recovering from a myocardial infarction cannot take a beta blocker and still has exertional angina. Her echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular function. What is accurate about adding diltiazem?
src.key: It relieves angina but does not lower mortality
src.explanation: Diltiazem and verapamil do not lower mortality after infarction; when a beta blocker cannot be used they relieve angina or control rate, provided function is preserved and there is no heart failure.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Definitions and the three syncope groups
items.html: Near-syncope. It precedes syncope, which is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness followed by spontaneous recovery.

src.question: A 35-year-old woman standing at an outdoor event in the heat develops tunnel vision, lightheadedness and dizziness but is still conscious. If her pressure keeps falling, what is likely to follow?
src.explanation: Her symptoms are near-syncope, which precedes syncope: a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness followed by spontaneous recovery.

items.html: Calculating non-high-density cholesterol. It is total cholesterol minus high-density cholesterol; for example, 250 minus 40 is 210 mg/dL.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 116

src.question: A 49-year-old man with hypertriglyceridemia has a total cholesterol of 250 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein of 40 mg/dL and triglyceride of 300 mg/dL. What is his non-high-density cholesterol?
src.explanation: Non-high-density cholesterol is total cholesterol minus high-density cholesterol: 250 minus 40 is 210 mg/dL.

items.html: Tricuspid stenosis referral. It is referred when seen on an echocardiogram or when there are heart failure related symptoms.

src.question: A 42-year-old woman has tricuspid stenosis seen on an echocardiogram and mild leg swelling. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Tricuspid stenosis is referred when it is seen on an echocardiogram or when there are heart failure related symptoms, both of which she has.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Orthostatic syncope: diagnosis and first-line care
items.html: Orthostatic syncope counseling. Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, and understanding why helps patients follow the advice.

src.question: A 79-year-old man with Parkinson disease faints when he gets up at night. His readings show a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
src.key: Sit first, then stand up slowly
src.explanation: Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, and understanding why helps him follow the advice.

items.html: Blood pressure measurement technique. No rest period, talking during measurement, a sleeved arm and crossed legs each inflate the reading, so a reading taken this way is repeated after five minutes of quiet rest; a diagnosis rests on readings taken to standard.

src.question: A 54-year-old arrives late for a routine visit, is taken straight to the room and has her blood pressure measured immediately while she describes her morning. The cuff is placed over her sleeve and her legs are crossed. The reading is 152/94. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Repeat it after five minutes of quiet rest
src.explanation: Every departure here inflates the reading: no rest period, talking during the measurement, a sleeved arm and crossed legs. A diagnosis rests on readings taken to standard, and acting on this one would start treatment on an artifact. Correct technique matters as much as the rest period.

items.html: Symptomatic orthostatic hypotension. Syncope is the result: when the standing pressure falls far enough, brain perfusion drops and consciousness is briefly lost.

src.question: A 70-year-old man on a newly increased diuretic keeps standing up quickly despite advice, and his pressure falls 30 mmHg on standing. If this continues, what is he most at risk of?
src.explanation: Syncope is the result of symptomatic hypotension: when the standing pressure falls far enough, brain perfusion drops and consciousness is briefly lost.

items.html: Implantable defibrillator criteria. The device is indicated only with a life expectancy of at least one year, together with ejection fraction 35% or less, class II or III and optimal therapy.

src.question: A 71-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy has an ejection fraction of 25%, is class II on optimal guideline-directed therapy, and has metastatic cancer with an expected survival of a few months. Which is most appropriate regarding an implantable defibrillator?
src.key: It is not indicated for him
src.explanation: The device is indicated only with a life expectancy of at least one year, together with ejection fraction 35% or less, class II or III and optimal therapy. His expected survival of months fails that criterion.

items.html: Goals of heart failure treatment. The goals are to decrease symptoms, increase survival and limit disease progression; feeling better meets only the first of the three.

src.question: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure asks why she must take several medicines when she already feels better. Which explanation matches the goals of treatment?
src.key: They also extend life and slow progression
src.explanation: The goals are to decrease symptoms, increase survival and limit disease progression. Feeling better meets only the first of the three, so the regimen continues.

items.html: Alcohol and blood pressure. Excess alcohol raises blood pressure chronically, and withdrawal from it can produce acute severe hypertension.

src.question: A 49-year-old man who drinks heavily is admitted for an unrelated procedure. On the second day his blood pressure rises sharply. What explains this?
src.key: Alcohol withdrawal can produce acute severe hypertension
src.explanation: and the relationship runs both ways: excess alcohol raises blood pressure chronically, and withdrawal from it can raise it acutely.

items.section_title: 5.9 · ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
items.html: Right ventricular infarct and nitroglycerin. The infarcted right ventricle is preload dependent; nitroglycerin decreases preload, reducing the Frank-Starling effect, so it fails into right-sided heart failure, output drops and shock follows.

src.question: Nitroglycerin is withheld in a right ventricular infarct because the injured right ventricle depends on what?
src.explanation: The infarcted right ventricle is preload dependent: nitroglycerin decreases preload, which reduces the Frank-Starling effect on its myocardium, so it fails into right-sided heart failure, output drops and shock follows.

also.explanation: The infarcted right ventricle is preload dependent; decreasing preload reduces the Frank-Starling effect, the ventricle fails into right-sided heart failure, output falls and shock follows.

items.html: Statins above age 75. In primary prevention the approach is clinical assessment and a risk discussion rather than an automatic prescription.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 96

src.question: An 81-year-old woman with no history of atherosclerotic disease asks whether she should start a statin for prevention. Her low-density lipoprotein is 145 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate approach?
src.explanation: Above 75 in primary prevention the approach is clinical assessment and a risk discussion rather than an automatic prescription.

items.html: Cardiogenic shock after infarction. It is more common in left-sided myocardial infarctions, and left ventricular involvement carries a higher mortality.

src.question: A 70-year-old man is admitted with a large myocardial infarction and develops hypotension, cool extremities and falling urine output from cardiogenic shock. Which infarct feature makes this complication more common?
src.explanation: Cardiogenic shock is more common in left-sided myocardial infarctions, and left ventricular involvement carries a higher mortality. The left ventricle supplies the systemic output that shock takes away.

items.html: Arrhythmia work-up in syncope. The work-up is an electrocardiogram, cardiac monitoring and a stress test, together with cardiology consultation.

src.question: A 75-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction heart failure faints abruptly while walking after a brief racing heartbeat. After his electrocardiogram, which further test helps capture an intermittent arrhythmia?
src.explanation: The arrhythmia work-up is an electrocardiogram, cardiac monitoring and a stress test, together with cardiology consultation.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Orthostatic syncope: diagnosis and first-line care
items.html: History in orthostatic syncope. History is the most important tool for finding the source, or for referring to the right specialty for confirmation when the source remains unclear.

src.question: A 63-year-old woman has recurrent lightheadedness on standing. Her orthostatic readings meet criteria, but her history does not make clear whether the cause is autonomic failure or something else. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.key: Refer to the right specialty to confirm
src.explanation: History is the most important tool for the source of orthostatic syncope, or for referring to the right specialty for confirmation when it remains unclear.

also.key: Referral to the right specialty to confirm
also.explanation: History is the most important tool for the diagnosis, or for referring to the right specialty for confirmation when the source is still unclear.

items.section_title: 5.5 · Troponin — the numbers you need to know
items.html: Troponin and disposition. Troponin is a tool that says who can safely go home: two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L, far below the men's 20 ng/L, with a normal electrocardiogram rule out an infarct.
cites: Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026 - SUPPLEMENT slide 72a

src.question: A 46-year-old man with six hours of atypical chest discomfort has a normal electrocardiogram and two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L. Which disposition is most appropriate?
src.explanation: Troponin is a tool that says who can safely go home. Two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L, far below the men's 20 ng/L, with a normal electrocardiogram rule out an infarct.

items.html: Nuclear stress test defects. A reversible perfusion defect indicates ischemia, while a non-reversible (fixed) defect indicates infarction.

src.question: A 66-year-old man with chest pain has a nuclear stress test showing a perfusion defect that does not reverse at rest. What does this fixed defect indicate?
src.explanation: On a nuclear stress test, a reversible perfusion defect indicates ischemia, while a non-reversible (fixed) defect indicates infarction.

items.html: Age as a coronary risk factor. Age becomes a nonmodifiable coronary risk factor at 45 or older for men and 55 or older for women.

src.question: A 52-year-old woman and her 52-year-old husband ask at a wellness visit whether their age already counts as a coronary risk factor. Which answer is accurate?
src.explanation: Age becomes a nonmodifiable coronary risk factor at 45 or older for men and 55 or older for women. At 52 he has crossed his threshold and she has not.

items.section_title: 5.5 · Troponin — the numbers you need to know
items.html: Serial troponin. When one troponin is drawn, two are needed: the change between draws is what matters, and a rising second value leads to a third as more cells die.
cites: Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026 - SUPPLEMENT slide 72a

src.question: Why is a second troponin drawn after the first?
src.explanation: When you get one, you have to get two: the change between draws is what matters, and a rising second value leads to a third as more cells die.

items.html: Coronary artery calcium scoring. In adults 40 to 75 without diabetes, with low-density lipoprotein of 70 to 189 and 10-year risk of 7.5% to 19.9%, it is considered when the statin decision is uncertain.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 106

src.question: A 57-year-old woman without diabetes has low-density lipoprotein of 140 mg/dL and a 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 10%. She is unsure whether to start a statin, and no risk enhancers are present. Which test can help the decision?
src.explanation: In adults 40 to 75 without diabetes, with low-density lipoprotein of 70 to 189 and 10-year risk of 7.5% to 19.9%, coronary artery calcium scoring is considered when the statin decision is uncertain.

items.html: Thiazide monitoring. Thiazides carry a risk of hyponatremia, particularly where sodium is already low-normal, and volume status matters in older adults too; electrolytes and uric acid are the standing monitoring for the class.

src.question: A 78-year-old woman is started on chlorthalidone. Which monitoring matters most for her?
src.key: Sodium, given the risk of thiazide hyponatremia
src.explanation: particularly where sodium is already low-normal, and volume status matters in older adults too. Electrolytes and uric acid are the standing monitoring for the class.

items.html: Renal artery stenosis referral. Recurrent flash pulmonary edema, progressive renal decline despite optimal therapy, and truly refractory control trigger early referral, rather than the mere presence of narrowing on imaging.

src.question: A 66-year-old with confirmed renal artery stenosis has recurrent flash pulmonary edema and progressive renal decline despite optimal medical therapy. What is the appropriate step?
src.explanation: Recurrent flash pulmonary edema, progressive renal decline despite optimal therapy, and truly refractory control are the three features that trigger early referral, rather than the mere presence of narrowing on imaging.

items.html: Congestive heart failure requires congestion. A clinical diagnosis requires congestion, meaning pulmonary or peripheral edema; symptoms and a mildly reduced ejection fraction without edema do not meet the congestive label.

src.question: A 73-year-old woman has grade II diastolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 46%. She has fatigue and breathlessness with exertion but has never had pulmonary or peripheral edema and has never needed a diuretic. Does she meet a clinical diagnosis of congestive heart failure?
src.explanation: A clinical diagnosis of congestive heart failure requires congestion, meaning pulmonary or peripheral edema. She has symptoms and a mildly reduced ejection fraction, but without edema the congestive label does not apply.

items.html: Tilt-table test sensitivity. With a sensitivity of about 40%, many patients with the syndrome test negative, so a negative result does not exclude it; a positive result, with specificity above 80%, carries more weight.

src.question: A 20-year-old woman has a classic history of palpitations and lightheadedness on standing that improve lying down, but her tilt-table test is negative. How should the negative result be interpreted?
src.key: It does not exclude the syndrome
src.explanation: With a sensitivity of about 40%, many patients with the syndrome test negative, so a negative result tells almost nothing; a positive result, with specificity above 80%, carries more weight.

also.key: It does little to exclude the syndrome
also.explanation: Low sensitivity means many patients with the syndrome test negative, so a negative result tells almost nothing, while a positive result carries more weight.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Orthostatic syncope: diagnosis and first-line care
items.html: Self-care in orthostatic syncope. Slow positional changes, with a pause sitting before standing, are listed treatment, alongside treating the underlying cause.

src.question: A 76-year-old woman with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from diabetes asks what she can do herself to stop fainting when she gets out of bed. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
src.explanation: Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, with a pause sitting before standing, alongside treatment of the underlying cause.

also.explanation: Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, alongside treating the underlying cause, the real diagnosis.

items.section_title: 5.4 · The chest pain workup and risk scores
items.html: Serial troponin I. Troponin is drawn serially: when one is drawn, a second follows, because the change over time is what matters; a rising troponin I would turn the presentation into an infarction.
cites: Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026.pptx, Slides 32, 47; Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026 - SUPPLEMENT slide 72a

src.question: A 59-year-old man had 30 minutes of chest pressure at rest. His electrocardiogram shows nonspecific T-wave changes, and his first troponin I is not abnormal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Troponin is drawn serially: when one is drawn, a second follows, because the change over time is what matters. A rising troponin I would turn this presentation into an infarction.

items.section_title: 5.3 · Angina pectoris: the pain, silent ischemia and referred pain
items.html: Angina pectoris. It is transient myocardial ischemia that is not long or severe enough to cause infarction, and its symptoms are recurrent.

src.question: Which statement defines angina pectoris?
src.explanation: Angina pectoris is transient myocardial ischemia that is not long or severe enough to cause infarction, and its symptoms are recurrent.

items.section_title: 5.3 · Angina pectoris: the pain, silent ischemia and referred pain
items.html: Position and angina. The pain of angina pectoris is not affected by position and typically worsens with exertion; pain that changes with position lowers the suspicion that it is cardiac.

src.question: How does body position affect the pain of angina pectoris?
src.explanation: The pain of angina pectoris is not affected by position; it typically worsens with exertion. Pain that changes with position lowers the suspicion that it is cardiac.

items.section_title: 5.4 · The chest pain workup and risk scores
items.html: Coronary calcium score. A cardiac computed tomography calcium score (0 to 400 or more, higher meaning higher risk) stratifies future risk; it is not a test for acute coronary syndrome.

src.question: What is a coronary calcium score used for?
src.explanation: A cardiac computed tomography calcium score (0 to 400 or more, higher meaning higher risk) stratifies future risk. It is not a test for acute coronary syndrome.

also.explanation: A cardiac computed tomography calcium score is a risk stratification tool, not a test for acute coronary syndrome. A higher score means higher future risk, not an infarct in progress.

items.html: Angina and exertion. Exercise and emotional stress raise myocardial oxygen demand; a narrowed artery cannot raise supply to match, and the mismatch produces pain.

src.question: Why does angina typically worsen with exertion?
src.explanation: Exercise and emotional stress raise myocardial oxygen demand; a narrowed artery cannot raise supply to match, so the supply and demand mismatch produces pain.

items.html: Unstable angina versus non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Elevated troponin or high-sensitivity troponin differentiates the infarction from unstable angina, in which troponin is normal; both can occur at rest.

src.question: What separates unstable angina from non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
src.explanation: Elevated troponin or high-sensitivity troponin is what differentiates non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction from unstable angina, in which troponin is normal. Both can occur at rest.

items.section_title: 5.5 · Troponin — the numbers you need to know
items.html: Interpreting serial troponin. Serial troponins are drawn to watch the change; a second high-sensitivity troponin I above the women's 99th percentile of 12 ng/L and higher than the first is rising and abnormal, so another is ordered.
cites: Coronary Artery Disease Carter 2026 - SUPPLEMENT slide 72a

src.question: A 59-year-old woman with chest pressure has a first high-sensitivity troponin I of 8 ng/L and a second, drawn later, of 30 ng/L. How should the second result be interpreted?
src.explanation: Serial troponins are drawn to watch the change. Her second high-sensitivity troponin I of 30 ng/L is above the women's 99th percentile of 12 ng/L and higher than the first, so another is ordered as cells continue to die.

items.html: Vasospastic angina diagnosis. The gold standard is coronary artery spasm provoked during angiography by ergonovine or acetylcholine, then resolved with nitroglycerin given through the catheter.

src.question: A 42-year-old man who smokes reports brief episodes of chest pain at rest in the early morning that resolve on their own. Coronary vasospasm is suspected. Which test is the gold standard for confirming the diagnosis?
src.explanation: The gold standard is coronary artery spasm provoked during angiography by ergonovine or acetylcholine, then resolved with nitroglycerin given through the catheter.

items.html: Change in stable angina. A change occurring at rest, new and limiting, or increasing in frequency and discomfort is unstable angina, an acute coronary syndrome and a medical emergency.

src.question: A 69-year-old woman with known stable angina says her chest pain now comes more often, lasts longer and appears with less exertion. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: A change in a patient's stable angina (occurring at rest, new and limiting, or increasing in frequency and discomfort) is unstable angina, an acute coronary syndrome and a medical emergency.

items.html: Nonmodifiable coronary risk factors. Age, sex and genetics (family history) cannot be changed, whereas hypertension, obesity and a sedentary lifestyle are modifiable.

src.question: A 57-year-old man with hypertension, obesity and a sedentary office job asks which of his coronary risk factors he cannot change. Which answer is accurate?
src.explanation: Age, sex and genetics (family history) are the nonmodifiable coronary risk factors. Hypertension, obesity and a sedentary lifestyle are all modifiable and are where his effort should go.

items.html: Aspirin in vasospastic angina. Aspirin is on the avoid list, together with nonselective beta blockers and triptans; prevention is a calcium channel blocker plus stopping smoking.

src.question: A 40-year-old man with vasospastic angina, now on a calcium channel blocker, read that daily aspirin prevents heart attacks and asks whether he should start it. What should he be told?
src.key: Aspirin is avoided in this condition
src.explanation: Aspirin is on the avoid list for vasospastic angina, together with nonselective beta blockers and triptans. His prevention is a calcium channel blocker plus stopping smoking.

items.html: Triptans in vasospastic angina. Triptans such as sumatriptan can precipitate coronary vasospasm and are on the avoid list, along with nonselective beta blockers and aspirin.

src.question: A 44-year-old woman with vasospastic angina also has migraines. Her medication list includes amlodipine, diltiazem, sublingual nitroglycerin and sumatriptan. Which medication should she avoid?
src.explanation: Triptans such as sumatriptan can precipitate coronary vasospasm and are on the avoid list for vasospastic angina, along with nonselective beta blockers and aspirin.

items.html: High-output heart failure. It is elevated cardiac output from increased heart rate and contractility, meeting an increased peripheral demand; over time it may lead to ischemic cardiomyopathy or remodeling.

src.question: What defines high-output heart failure?
src.key: Elevated output from faster rate and contraction
src.explanation: High-output failure is elevated cardiac output from increased heart rate and contractility, meeting an increased peripheral demand; over time it may lead to ischemic cardiomyopathy or remodeling.

items.html: Diagnosing congestive heart failure. It is a clinical diagnosis: signs and symptoms of heart failure plus an elevated B-type natriuretic peptide or cardiogenic pulmonary or systemic congestion; no single test makes the diagnosis alone.

src.question: How is congestive heart failure diagnosed?
src.key: Clinically, from signs and symptoms plus supporting evidence
src.explanation: Congestive heart failure is a clinical diagnosis: signs and symptoms of heart failure plus an elevated B-type natriuretic peptide or cardiogenic pulmonary or systemic congestion. No single test makes the diagnosis alone.

items.html: Reduced ejection fraction therapy. Core therapy is a beta blocker, a renin-angiotensin blocker such as lisinopril, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone and a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin, with diuretics as needed.

src.question: Which combination reflects core therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
src.explanation: The core is a beta blocker, a renin-angiotensin blocker such as lisinopril (or an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor, converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker), a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist such as spironolactone and a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin, with diuretics as needed.

items.html: High-output heart failure treatment. It is driven by peripheral demand, so treatment targets the cause, such as anemia, hyperthyroidism or an arteriovenous fistula, with a diuretic for congestion.

src.question: How is high-output heart failure treated?
src.key: Treat the underlying cause and add a diuretic
src.explanation: High-output failure is driven by peripheral demand, so treatment targets the cause, such as anemia, hyperthyroidism or an arteriovenous fistula, with a diuretic for congestion.

items.html: Defibrillator vest. The vest covers the period in which guideline-directed therapy is optimized and cardiac rehabilitation is completed; the echocardiogram is then repeated to decide whether an implantable device is needed.

src.question: A 57-year-old woman recovering from acute heart failure after an infarction, with an ejection fraction of 31%, asks why she must wear a defibrillator vest. Which explanation is accurate?
src.key: It protects her while therapy is optimized
src.explanation: The vest covers the period in which guideline-directed therapy is optimized and she completes cardiac rehabilitation; the echocardiogram is then repeated to decide whether she needs an implantable device.

items.html: B-type natriuretic peptide rule-out. A level below 100 rules out acute heart failure with a negative predictive value above 90%, so breathlessness then needs another explanation.

src.question: A 55-year-old woman has breathlessness on exertion for a week. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 45. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: A level below 100 rules out acute heart failure with a negative predictive value above 90%, so her breathlessness needs another explanation.

items.html: Hypertension prevalence. Close to half of adults (47.7 percent) have hypertension, using the threshold of 130/80 or current antihypertensive treatment.

src.question: What proportion of adults have hypertension by current national survey data?
src.explanation: at 47.7 percent using the threshold of 130/80 or current antihypertensive treatment. It is the single number that explains why this condition dominates primary care.

items.html: Hypertension control. Among adults with hypertension only about one in five (20.7 percent) achieves below 130/80; awareness and treatment figures are far higher, so the gap is between being treated and being controlled.

src.question: Among adults with hypertension, what does the control figure show?
src.key: Only about one in five reaches the target
src.explanation: at 20.7 percent achieving below 130/80. Awareness and treatment figures are both far higher, so the gap is between being treated and being controlled rather than between being ill and being diagnosed.

items.html: Blood pressure in both arms. It is measured in both arms at the initial visit to find a difference, and the higher consistent arm is used subsequently; an asymmetric reading also raises concern for acute aortic pathology.

src.question: Why is blood pressure measured in both arms at the initial visit?
src.key: To find a difference and pick the arm for follow-up
src.explanation: the higher consistent arm is used subsequently. An asymmetric reading is also one of the examination findings that raises concern for acute aortic pathology.

items.html: Kidney disease in hypertension. Other renal causes such as diabetes must be excluded, since attributing everything to pressure risks missing a treatable second disease; the relationship is bidirectional, so the presence of both does not establish which came first.

src.question: Why should not all chronic kidney disease in a hypertensive patient be attributed to blood pressure?
src.key: Other renal causes such as diabetes must be excluded
src.explanation: Attributing everything to the pressure risks missing a treatable second disease, and the relationship is bidirectional anyway, so the presence of both does not establish which came first.

items.html: Coarctation of the aorta. Suspect it with upper-extremity hypertension and weak or delayed femoral pulses; comparing arm with leg pressures confirms it, since normally the leg systolic is higher and a reversal is the telling finding.

src.question: What clinical finding should raise suspicion of coarctation of the aorta?
src.key: Upper-extremity hypertension with weak or delayed femoral pulses
src.explanation: and the confirmation is to compare arm with leg pressures: normally the leg systolic is the higher of the two, so a reversal of that relationship is the telling finding.

items.html: Pressure reduction in hypertensive emergency. Mean arterial pressure is reduced by no more than about 20 to 25 percent in the first hour, targeting around 160/100 to 110 over two to six hours; aortic dissection and some stroke syndromes are excepted.

src.question: By how much should mean arterial pressure be reduced in the first hour of a hypertensive emergency?
src.key: By no more than about twenty to twenty-five percent
src.explanation: with a target around 160/100 to 110 over two to six hours and gradual normalization over a day or two. Aortic dissection and some stroke syndromes are excepted from this general approach.

items.html: Hypertension and stroke. Hypertension predisposes to both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke; chronic small-vessel injury separately contributes to white matter change, lacunar infarcts and cognitive decline.

src.question: Which cerebrovascular events does hypertension predispose to?
src.explanation: It raises the risk of both mechanisms rather than one, and chronic small-vessel injury separately contributes to white matter change, lacunar infarcts and cognitive decline.

also.explanation: Hypertension raises the risk of both mechanisms, and chronic small-vessel injury separately contributes to white matter change, lacunar infarcts and cognitive decline.

items.html: Modifiable risk factors for hypertension. These are excess weight, high sodium, inactivity and alcohol, with low potassium intake and poor sleep also on the list; each maps onto a lifestyle intervention, recommended at every blood pressure category.

src.question: Which modifiable factors raise the risk of developing hypertension?
src.key: Excess weight, high sodium, inactivity and alcohol
src.explanation: and each maps onto a lifestyle intervention, which is why lifestyle treatment is recommended at every blood pressure category rather than only once medication has begun. Low potassium intake and poor sleep belong on the list too.

items.html: Pheochromocytoma. Catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction produces volume contraction, so the patient can be hypertensive and orthostatic at once.

src.question: Why might a patient with pheochromocytoma have orthostatic symptoms despite being hypertensive?
src.explanation: and it is a genuinely counterintuitive combination: the same catecholamine excess that raises the pressure also shrinks the circulating volume, so the patient is hypertensive and orthostatic at once.

items.html: First-line drugs for uncomplicated hypertension. They are thiazide diuretics, renin-angiotensin blockers (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers) and dihydropyridines; beta blockers are reserved for comorbidities such as reduced ejection fraction or ischemic disease.

src.question: Which drug classes are first-line for uncomplicated hypertension?
src.key: Thiazide diuretics, renin-angiotensin blockers and dihydropyridines
src.explanation: and beta blockers are deliberately absent from that list: they are reserved for patients whose comorbidities, such as reduced ejection fraction or ischemic disease, select them. That means angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers among the three.

items.html: Hypertensive emergency. Mean arterial pressure falls by no more than about 20 to 25 percent in the first hour; autoregulation has adapted to the higher pressure, so an acute drop to a chronic goal can cause ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.

src.question: A 62-year-old man arrives with blood pressure 232/128, confusion and blurred vision. Over the first hour, how far should his mean arterial pressure be reduced?
src.key: By no more than about twenty to twenty-five percent
src.explanation: targeting around 160/100 to 110 over two to six hours and gradual normalization over a day or two. Autoregulation has adapted to the higher pressure, so dropping it to a chronic goal acutely can cause ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.

items.html: Hypertensive heart disease. A normal ejection fraction does not reassure, because preserved-fraction failure is one of the two routes hypertensive heart disease can take.

src.question: A 67-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has echocardiography showing left ventricular hypertrophy with impaired diastolic relaxation and a normal ejection fraction. He is breathless on exertion. What does this mean for his prognosis?
src.key: Preserved ejection fraction failure is a recognized endpoint
src.explanation: A normal ejection fraction does not reassure, because preserved-fraction failure is one of the two routes hypertensive heart disease can take.

items.html: Clues to secondary hypertension. Early or abrupt onset, resistance, or lost control should prompt a search for a secondary cause, since each departs from the gradual course expected of primary hypertension.

src.question: Which pattern of hypertension should prompt a search for a secondary cause?
src.key: Early or abrupt onset, resistance, or lost control
src.explanation: Each departs from the gradual course expected of primary hypertension, which is what makes the pattern itself the clue rather than any single reading.

items.html: Home blood pressure readings. The average matters, not one reading; overreacting to an outlier generates anxiety and unnecessary changes in therapy, so the schedule is built around averaging fourteen readings.

src.question: A 47-year-old woman starting home monitoring calls alarmed because one reading was 168/102, although her seven-day average is 128/80. What should she be told?
src.key: Reassure her that the average matters, not one reading
src.explanation: Overreacting to an outlier generates anxiety and unnecessary changes in therapy, which is why the schedule is built around averaging fourteen readings.

items.html: Diagnosing reflex syncope. History is the most important portion, summed up as history, history, history, with a log of pattern and frequency.

src.question: How is reflex syncope diagnosed?
src.explanation: History is the most important portion of diagnosing reflex syncope, summed up as history, history, history, with a log of pattern and frequency.

items.html: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Inadequate norepinephrine release from sympathetic postganglionic neurons means the vessels fail to constrict and the heart rate rises less than expected.

src.question: Why does pressure fall on standing in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
src.key: Too little norepinephrine from sympathetic nerves
src.explanation: Inadequate norepinephrine release from sympathetic postganglionic neurons means the vessels fail to constrict and the heart rate rises less than expected.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Definitions and the three syncope groups
items.html: Symptomatic hypotension. Low peripheral resistance or low cardiac output lowers pressure until brain perfusion falls and consciousness is briefly lost, which is syncope.

src.question: What does symptomatic hypotension lead to?
src.explanation: Syncope is the result of symptomatic hypotension: low peripheral resistance or low cardiac output lowers pressure until brain perfusion falls and consciousness is briefly lost.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Definitions and the three syncope groups
items.html: Near-syncope versus syncope. Near-syncope, or presyncope, is the dizziness, lightheadedness and tunnel vision that precede a faint; syncope adds the transient loss of consciousness and postural tone.

src.question: What separates near-syncope from syncope?
src.explanation: Near-syncope, or presyncope, is the dizziness, lightheadedness and tunnel vision that precede a faint; syncope adds the transient loss of consciousness and postural tone.

items.html: Micturition syncope. Alcohol and relative dehydration predispose to it, and reflex hypotension is managed by reducing or removing the trigger.

src.question: A 74-year-old man had a faint while urinating at night after an evening of drinking alcohol and little water. He takes an alpha-1 blocker and lisinopril. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
src.explanation: Alcohol and relative dehydration predispose him to micturition syncope, and reflex hypotension is managed by reducing or removing the trigger.

items.html: Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Poor intake and dehydration are listed causes, and treatment aims at the underlying cause, such as volume loss.

src.question: A 64-year-old man is recovering from a stomach virus that left him eating and drinking little. He fainted on standing, and orthostatic readings show a large pressure fall with a brisk heart rate rise. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
src.key: Keep up fluids while intake is poor
src.explanation: Poor intake and dehydration are listed causes of non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and treating the underlying cause, here the volume loss, is the aim.

items.html: Pulmonic regurgitation cause. Significant pulmonic regurgitation is most often iatrogenic: surgical valvotomy, valvectomy or valvuloplasty done to relieve right ventricular outflow tract obstruction leaves the valve leaking.

src.question: What is the most common cause of significant pulmonic regurgitation?
src.explanation: Significant pulmonic regurgitation is most often iatrogenic: surgical valvotomy, valvectomy or valvuloplasty done to relieve right ventricular outflow tract obstruction leaves the valve leaking.

also.explanation: Iatrogenic regurgitation, after surgical valvotomy, valvectomy or valvuloplasty to reduce right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, is the most common cause of significant pulmonic regurgitation.

items.html: Chronic mitral regurgitation. It dilates the left ventricle with eccentric hypertrophy, causing left heart failure, then pulmonary hypertension, and finally combined right and left heart failure.

src.question: How does chronic mitral regurgitation progress?
src.key: Left heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, then both sides fail
src.explanation: Chronic mitral regurgitation dilates the left ventricle with eccentric hypertrophy, causing left heart failure, then pulmonary hypertension, and finally combined right and left heart failure.

items.html: Pulmonic regurgitation discovery. It is usually an incidental finding on an echocardiogram or physical examination; management is to treat the underlying condition.

src.question: How is pulmonic regurgitation usually discovered?
src.explanation: Pulmonic regurgitation is usually an incidental finding on an echocardiogram or on physical examination; management is to treat the underlying condition.

items.html: Mechanical heart valve. It needs lifelong anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist, most commonly warfarin, monitored against an international normalized ratio target.

src.question: What should a patient receiving a mechanical heart valve be told about anticoagulation?
src.key: It will be needed for life
src.explanation: A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist, most commonly warfarin, monitored against an international normalized ratio target.

items.html: Aortic stenosis and nitrates. Patients are preload dependent and nitrates drop preload, so nitrates are avoided if angina is present; the same logic removes dehydration and strenuous exertion.

src.question: A 76-year-old man with known severe aortic stenosis has exertional chest pain. His physician is reviewing options before cardiology sees him. Which should be avoided for his chest pain?
src.explanation: Patients with aortic stenosis are preload dependent, and nitrates drop preload. If angina is present in aortic stenosis, nitrates are avoided; the same logic removes dehydration and strenuous exertion.

items.html: Tricuspid regurgitation referral. It is referred when identified on echocardiogram or when there are right heart failure symptoms; pedal edema and ascites mark severe disease.

src.question: A 66-year-old woman has tricuspid regurgitation identified on an echocardiogram and now has pedal edema and ascites. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Tricuspid regurgitation is referred when it is identified on echocardiogram or when there are right heart failure symptoms; pedal edema and ascites mark severe disease.

items.html: Mitral stenosis follow-up. All patients with evidence of mitral stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult to evaluate them and set the frequency of follow-up. Asymptomatic disease in sinus rhythm needs no therapy yet.

src.question: A 36-year-old woman has mitral stenosis found on an echocardiogram done before pregnancy. She has no symptoms and is in sinus rhythm. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: All patients with evidence of mitral stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult to evaluate them and set the frequency of follow-up. Asymptomatic disease in sinus rhythm needs no therapy yet.

items.html: Medical management of mitral regurgitation. Treatment aims to increase forward cardiac output while reducing regurgitant volume, and to treat comorbidities such as atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension.

src.question: A 70-year-old man with chronic mitral regurgitation also has atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension. He is not yet a surgical candidate. Which is part of his medical management?
src.explanation: Medical treatment of mitral regurgitation aims to increase forward cardiac output while reducing regurgitant volume, and to treat comorbidities such as atrial fibrillation and pulmonary hypertension.

items.html: Pulmonic regurgitation referral. Pulmonic regurgitation is referred to cardiology when it is seen on echocardiogram or when there are right heart failure signs and symptoms.

src.question: A 52-year-old woman has pulmonic regurgitation on echocardiogram and has developed leg edema and distended neck veins. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Pulmonic regurgitation is referred when it is seen on echocardiogram or when there are right heart failure signs and symptoms, both of which she has.

items.html: Tricuspid stenosis management. Severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis is managed with a low-salt diet together with diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist, which limits the systemic venous congestion.

src.question: A 46-year-old woman is diagnosed with severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis and asks what she can do at home. Which advice is most appropriate?
src.explanation: Severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis is managed with a low-salt diet together with diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist, which limits the systemic venous congestion.

items.html: Dilated aortic root. Patients with a dilated aortic root should be monitored by a cardiologist. A patient with an audible regurgitant murmur should have a cardiology consult to decide whether follow-up is needed.

src.question: A 41-year-old man has an echocardiogram showing a dilated aortic root with mild aortic regurgitation. He feels well. Which is the most appropriate plan?
src.explanation: Patients with a dilated aortic root should be monitored by a cardiologist, and a patient with an audible regurgitant murmur should have a cardiology consult to decide whether follow-up is needed.

items.html: Pulmonic stenosis referral. Whether congenital or related to heart failure, pulmonic stenosis present on echocardiogram should be referred to a cardiologist.

src.question: A 21-year-old woman has pulmonic stenosis seen incidentally on an echocardiogram. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Whether congenital or related to heart failure, pulmonic stenosis present on echocardiogram should be referred to a cardiologist.

items.html: Lipoprotein(a). It is similar to low-density lipoprotein in lipid and protein composition but carries apolipoprotein(a) as well as apolipoprotein B-100.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 7

src.question: Which feature distinguishes lipoprotein(a) from low-density lipoprotein?
src.key: It carries apolipoprotein(a) as well as B-100
src.explanation: Lipoprotein(a) is similar to low-density lipoprotein in lipid and protein composition but carries a distinct protein, apolipoprotein(a), in addition to apolipoprotein B-100.

items.section_title: 3.6 · Secondary causes, and what to rule out before a statin
items.html: Primary causes of dyslipidemia. Even after secondary causes are excluded, primary causes are sought because they affect management of family members, who may carry the same disorder, as well as coronary risk and drug response.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 94

src.question: Once secondary causes are excluded, why should primary causes still be sought?
src.key: They affect management of family members
src.explanation: Primary causes influence the risk of developing coronary disease, the response to drug therapy and the management of other family members, who may carry the same disorder.

items.html: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome. Eruptive xanthomas, small yellowish-white papules, cluster on the back, buttocks and extensor surfaces of the arms and legs, alongside lipemia retinalis and pancreatitis.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 44

src.question: Where do the eruptive xanthomas of familial chylomicronemia syndrome cluster?
src.explanation: They are clusters of small yellowish-white papules on the back, buttocks and extensor surfaces of the arms and legs, alongside lipemia retinalis and pancreatitis.

items.html: Adding to a maximal statin. Ezetimibe is added before the injectable class such as evolocumab; adding evolocumab before ezetimibe is out of sequence and less cost-effective.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 97

src.question: A 66-year-old man with a prior heart attack and symptomatic peripheral arterial disease takes a maximal statin, and his low-density lipoprotein is 82 mg/dL. Which change is inappropriate at this point?
src.explanation: If the injectable class is considered, ezetimibe is added to the maximal statin before it; skipping that step is out of sequence and less cost-effective.

items.html: Elevated lipoprotein(a). It is a causal and independent risk factor for atherosclerotic disease, so these patients need aggressive therapy to decrease low-density lipoprotein.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 7

src.question: A 58-year-old man whose brother had a heart attack at 50 has lipoprotein(a) measured at 85 mg/dL. His low-density lipoprotein is 140 mg/dL. What does the lipoprotein(a) result mean for his management?
src.explanation: Elevated lipoprotein(a) is a causal and independent risk factor for atherosclerotic disease, and a patient with it needs aggressive therapy to decrease low-density lipoprotein.

items.html: Diagnosing familial hypercholesterolemia. No definitive diagnostic test exists for the heterozygous form; skin biopsy with receptor activity confirms only the homozygous disorder.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 52

src.question: A 36-year-old woman has just been told she has heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. She asks whether any single test can prove it. Which answer is accurate?
src.key: No definitive test exists for her form
src.explanation: No definitive diagnostic test is available for the heterozygous form; the skin biopsy with receptor activity confirms only the homozygous disorder.

items.html: Fasting for lipid panels. Under the 2018 guideline a non-fasting panel, calculated low-density value included, is acceptable for routine screening; a fasting repeat is needed only when triglyceride is 400 mg/dL or more.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 66

src.question: A 40-year-old woman had a routine lipid panel drawn two hours after breakfast, and the order included triglyceride and a calculated low-density lipoprotein. Her triglyceride is 160 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Under the 2018 guideline a non-fasting panel is acceptable for routine screening, calculated low-density value included; a fasting repeat is needed only when triglyceride is 400 mg/dL or more.

items.html: Response to increased metabolic demand in heart failure. The body raises heart rate, contractility and preload; these help at first and later drive damage.

src.question: How does the body respond to increased metabolic demand in heart failure?
src.key: Raises heart rate, contractility and preload
src.explanation: Neurohormonal input raises the heart rate, catecholamines and autonomic input raise contractility, and venous capacitance and renal compensation augment preload. These help at first and later drive damage.

items.html: Lipid screening in children. Elective lipid screening is appropriate for patients as young as 2 years old with a family history of heart disease or high cholesterol.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 66

src.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought for a routine visit. His father had a heart attack at 40 and was found to have very high cholesterol. What is the most appropriate step regarding the boy's lipids?
src.explanation: Elective screening is appropriate for patients as young as 2 years old with a family history of heart disease or high cholesterol.

items.html: Building antihypertensive therapy. The foundational three are a renin-angiotensin blocker, a dihydropyridine and a thiazide-type diuretic; if still above goal on the first two at maximally tolerated doses, add a thiazide-type diuretic.

src.question: A 53-year-old man on an angiotensin receptor blocker and a dihydropyridine remains above goal at maximally tolerated doses. What is the next step?
src.explanation: The foundational three are a renin-angiotensin blocker, a dihydropyridine and a thiazide-type diuretic, all titrated before resistance can be considered confirmed. It is the third of the foundational agents.

items.html: Angioedema with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. It is a bradykinin-mediated class effect, two to four times more common in Black patients; an angiotensin receptor blocker is usually substituted.

src.question: A 48-year-old Black man develops lip and tongue swelling three months after starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. What should be known about this?
src.key: It is two to four times more common in this group
src.explanation: It is a bradykinin-mediated class effect of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition. Angiotensin receptor blockers can usually be used instead, though angioedema with them remains possible. An angiotensin receptor blocker is usually substituted.

items.html: Aortic dissection and pulses. Normal pulses do not exclude dissection; a normal pulse examination must not close the question, and imaging is still driven by clinical suspicion.

src.question: A 61-year-old with abrupt severe interscapular pain has symmetric, normal-volume pulses in all four limbs. What follows?
src.key: Normal pulses do not exclude dissection
src.explanation: Absent pulse findings specifically do not exclude the diagnosis, which is why a normal pulse examination must not close the question. Imaging is still driven by the clinical suspicion.

items.html: Apparent resistant hypertension. Medication nonadherence is the commonest explanation to exclude first, ahead of measurement error, white coat effect, high sodium or alcohol intake, interfering drugs, and undiagnosed sleep apnea or secondary hypertension.

src.question: A 59-year-old man remains at 158/96 on three agents at maximally tolerated doses. What is the commonest explanation to exclude first?
src.explanation: and it heads a list that also includes measurement error, white coat effect, high sodium or alcohol intake, interfering drugs, and undiagnosed sleep apnea or secondary hypertension.

also.explanation: and it heads a list that also includes measurement error, white coat effect, high sodium or alcohol intake, interfering drugs, and undiagnosed sleep apnea or secondary hypertension.

items.html: Dilated versus hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Dilated is thin, ballooned muscle that contracts poorly with loss of elasticity; hypertrophic is increased muscle that contracts strongly but relaxes poorly.

src.question: How does dilated cardiomyopathy differ from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
src.key: Thin, ballooned muscle that contracts poorly
src.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy is decreased muscle with poor contraction and loss of elasticity. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is increased muscle that contracts strongly but relaxes poorly.

items.html: Statin follow-up. Adherence and percentage response are assessed with a repeat lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks after starting a statin, then every 3 to 12 months as needed.
cites: 22. Atherosclerosis and Lipid Disorders 2026 Carter.pptx, Slide 107

src.question: A 59-year-old woman started a moderate-intensity statin six weeks ago for primary prevention. She feels well. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Adherence and percentage response are assessed with a repeat lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks after starting a statin, then every 3 to 12 months as needed; six weeks falls in that window.

items.html: Combined right and left heart failure. It is managed with symptom control, comfort care and heart transplant; when optimized therapy no longer controls symptoms, transplant evaluation or comfort care is discussed.

src.question: A 64-year-old man has combined right and left heart failure with symptoms at rest despite optimized guideline-directed therapy. Which course is most appropriate to discuss?
src.explanation: Combined right and left failure is managed with symptom control, comfort care and heart transplant. When optimized therapy no longer controls symptoms, those are the options to raise.

items.section_title: 4.12 · Test tips: the nine murmurs side by side
items.html: Mitral regurgitation murmur with handgrip. It becomes louder with squatting and handgrip, because raised peripheral vascular resistance to ventricular ejection pushes more regurgitation back into the left atrium.

src.question: A 59-year-old man has a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. He is asked to squeeze a hand grip firmly for a minute while the examiner listens. How does the murmur change?
src.explanation: Squatting and handgrip increase the mitral regurgitation murmur: peripheral vascular resistance to ventricular ejection rises and pushes more regurgitation back into the left atrium.

items.section_title: 5.10 · Catheterization, stents and bypass — words have meaning
items.html: Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy after a stent. Stopping a P2Y12 receptor antagonist such as clopidogrel plus aspirin in the first 6 weeks is the strongest predictor of stent thrombosis, a sudden clot in the stent that can cause a large, often fatal infarction.

src.question: A 57-year-old man had a drug-eluting stent placed two weeks ago for an acute coronary syndrome. He tells you the clopidogrel is expensive and he plans to stop it because his chest pain is gone. What should he be told?
src.key: Stopping now risks a clot in the stent
src.explanation: Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy (a P2Y12 receptor antagonist such as clopidogrel plus aspirin) in the first 6 weeks after a stent is the strongest predictor of stent thrombosis, a sudden clot that occludes the stent and can cause a large, often fatal infarction.

items.html: Mechanical valve and warfarin interruption. If surgery requires interrupting warfarin, bridge with heparin until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic; stopping warfarin with no bridge, leaving the valve uncovered, is to be avoided.

src.question: A 60-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve on warfarin is scheduled for a colectomy that requires stopping it. Which plan should be avoided?
src.explanation: If surgery requires interrupting warfarin, it must be bridged with heparin until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic; leaving a mechanical valve uncovered is the thing to avoid.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Orthostatic syncope: diagnosis and first-line care
items.html: Orthostatic syncope management. First-line care is slow position changes and treating the underlying cause; drugs come in when these are not enough.

src.question: A 67-year-old woman with diabetic autonomic neuropathy has recently begun fainting on standing. She has no supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat), heart disease or kidney disease. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
src.key: Slow position changes, treat the cause
src.explanation: Slow positional changes and treatment of the underlying condition are first-line for orthostatic syncope; drugs come in when these are not enough.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Definitions and the three syncope groups
items.html: Syncope defined. A transient, self-limited, brief loss of consciousness with inability to maintain postural tone, followed by spontaneous recovery, meaning full recovery.

src.question: Which description defines syncope?
