src.key: Brief loss of consciousness, then full recovery
src.explanation: Syncope is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness with inability to maintain postural tone, followed by spontaneous recovery.

items.section_title: 4.12 · Test tips: the nine murmurs side by side
items.html: Mitral regurgitation murmur with standing. It becomes softer with standing or the Valsalva maneuver and increases with squatting and handgrip, which raise resistance to ventricular ejection.

src.question: A 62-year-old woman has a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. She stands up quickly from squatting while the examiner listens. How does the murmur change?
src.explanation: The mitral regurgitation murmur decreases with standing or the Valsalva maneuver and increases with squatting and handgrip, which raise resistance to ventricular ejection.

items.html: Blood pressure goal. Intensify therapy when average blood pressure is above the goal of below 130/80, since values closer to 120/80 are encouraged where appropriate; the same threshold defines the condition and measures control.

src.question: A 54-year-old woman on two agents has an average blood pressure of 134/84. What should happen?
src.key: Intensify therapy, since the goal is below 130/80
src.explanation: and values closer to 120/80 are encouraged where appropriate. The same threshold defines the condition and measures control.

items.html: Vasovagal syncope triggers. Emotional stress, fear, pain, heat exposure or standing for a long time trigger it, and trigger avoidance is its treatment.

src.question: Which triggers are typical of vasovagal syncope?
src.key: Fear, pain, heat or prolonged standing
src.explanation: Vasovagal syncope is triggered by emotional stress, fear, pain, heat exposure or standing for a long time, and trigger avoidance is its treatment.

items.html: Syncope work-up. A blood glucose level rules out hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause; blood counts and a metabolic panel address infection and metabolic causes.

src.question: A 76-year-old man is seen in the emergency department after fainting while voiding at night. His examination is normal. Which test excludes hypoglycemia as the cause?
src.explanation: A normal blood glucose rules out hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause, as blood counts and a metabolic panel address infection and metabolic causes.

also.explanation: A normal blood glucose rules out hypoglycemia, one of the non-hypotensive causes of syncope, alongside blood counts and a metabolic panel for infection or metabolic causes.

items.html: Hyperthyroidism and ischemia. Myocardial ischemia is a mismatch between oxygen demand and supply, and hyperthyroidism raises the heart's oxygen demand, as do exercise, emotional stress, left ventricular hypertrophy, hyperthermia and cocaine.

src.question: A 45-year-old woman with untreated hyperthyroidism has chest pressure whenever she climbs stairs. She asks how her thyroid condition could cause chest pain. Which explanation is most accurate?
src.key: It raises the heart's oxygen demand
src.explanation: Myocardial ischemia is a mismatch between oxygen demand and supply. Hyperthyroidism sits on the increased-demand side, with exercise, emotional stress, left ventricular hypertrophy, hyperthermia and cocaine.

items.html: Modifiable heart failure risk factors. Tobacco, excess alcohol and obesity can be changed; age, family history and genetic abnormality cannot.

src.question: Which heart failure risk factors can a patient change?
src.explanation: These are modifiable, so they are the targets of prevention counseling. Age, family history and genetic abnormality are risk factors a patient cannot change.

items.html: Complete metabolic panel in heart failure. It follows potassium and renal function (blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and filtration rate), because diuretics and several therapies move potassium and affect the kidneys.

src.question: Why is a complete metabolic panel ordered in heart failure?
src.key: To follow potassium and renal function
src.explanation: The panel tracks electrolytes, potassium above all, and renal function through blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and filtration rate. Both matter because diuretics and several therapies move potassium and affect the kidneys.

items.html: Heart failure defined. The heart cannot pump blood at a rate that meets the body's metabolic needs at rest and during effort, or manages it only at abnormally high filling pressures.

src.question: Which description defines heart failure?
src.key: Output below demand, or met only at high filling pressures
src.explanation: The heart cannot pump blood at a rate that meets the body's metabolic needs at rest and during effort, or manages it only because filling pressures are abnormally high. That second half is why a normal output does not exclude the syndrome.

items.html: Monitoring on a loop diuretic. Potassium and kidney function are followed on the metabolic panel, because loop diuretics waste potassium.

src.question: What should a patient starting a loop diuretic expect to have monitored?
src.explanation: Loop diuretics waste potassium, so potassium and renal function are followed on the metabolic panel. The same monitoring applies in the other direction for the potassium-sparing antagonists.

items.html: Mitral stenosis murmur. A rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex with an opening snap; mitral stenosis is one of three causes of right-sided failure, with chronic left-sided failure and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

src.question: Which murmur accompanies mitral stenosis as a cause of right-sided heart failure?
src.key: Diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap
src.explanation: Mitral stenosis gives a rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex with an opening snap. It is one of the three causes of right-sided failure, alongside chronic left-sided failure and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

items.html: Heart failure stage C. Stage C is symptomatic structural heart disease, past or current; once symptoms have occurred, resolution on treatment does not move the patient backward, so the patient remains in stage C.

src.question: A 68-year-old woman was hospitalized last year for heart failure with edema. On treatment she is now symptom-free and asks whether she has moved back to stage B. Which reply is accurate?
src.explanation: Stage C is symptomatic structural heart disease, past or current. Once symptoms have occurred, resolution on treatment does not move the stage backward.

items.html: Defibrillator after infarction. The implantable defibrillator is placed only if the repeat echocardiogram shows no improvement; with an ejection fraction well above the 35% threshold, continue therapy without a device.

src.question: A 55-year-old man wore a defibrillator vest after an infarction while his guideline-directed therapy was optimized and he completed cardiac rehabilitation. His repeat echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 47%. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: The implantable defibrillator is placed only if the repeat echocardiogram shows no improvement. At 47% his fraction is well above the 35% threshold, so therapy continues without a device.

items.html: Thiazide-type diuretic choice. Chlorthalidone is preferred, with electrolytes and urate monitored: hyponatremia and hypokalemia are the electrolyte concerns, hyperuricemia may precipitate gout, and volume depletion matters especially in older adults.

src.question: Which thiazide-type diuretic is preferred, and what is monitored?
src.key: Chlorthalidone, with electrolytes and urate monitored
src.explanation: Hyponatremia and hypokalemia are the electrolyte concerns, hyperuricemia may precipitate gout, and volume depletion matters especially in older adults. Volume status is watched as well, particularly in older adults.

items.html: Obstructive sleep apnea and blood pressure. Recurrent airway obstruction causes repeated hypoxemia and arousal; intermittent hypoxemia drives sympathetic activation, which persists into waking hours.

src.question: By what mechanism does obstructive sleep apnea raise blood pressure?
src.explanation: Recurrent airway obstruction produces repeated hypoxemia and arousal, and the resulting sympathetic drive persists into waking hours rather than resolving with the night.

items.html: Baseline studies in new hypertension. Obtain renal function, electrolytes, glucose, lipids and urinalysis, with urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, thyroid-stimulating hormone and a full blood count; they screen for secondary causes, measure organ damage and set a baseline before drugs are started.

src.question: A 45-year-old man is newly diagnosed with hypertension. Which baseline studies are obtained?
src.key: Renal function, electrolytes, glucose, lipids and urinalysis
src.explanation: with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio alongside the creatinine. The panel does three jobs at once: screens for secondary causes, measures organ damage, and establishes a baseline before drugs that alter potassium and renal function are started. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and a full blood count complete it.

items.html: Hypertension needing immediate evaluation. Abrupt severe headache with a new focal neurological deficit, like confusion or seizures, visual disturbance, chest or severe back pain, and oliguria, maps to an organ under acute injury.

src.question: Which of these findings in a hypertensive patient requires immediate evaluation?
src.key: Abrupt severe headache with a new focal neurological deficit
src.explanation: Confusion or seizures, visual disturbance or focal deficit, abrupt severe headache, chest or severe back pain, and oliguria each map to an organ under acute injury.

items.html: Fundoscopy in hypertension. It allows direct visualization of the microvasculature; retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk, retinal arterial narrowing predicts future hypertension, and control can produce regression.

src.question: Why is fundoscopy performed in every newly diagnosed hypertensive patient?
src.key: It allows direct visualization of the microvasculature
src.explanation: and the findings carry prognostic weight beyond the reading itself: retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk, retinal arterial narrowing predicts future hypertension, and control can produce regression.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Definitions and the three syncope groups
items.html: Course of syncope. A syncopal episode is brief and self-limited, followed by spontaneous recovery, which helps separate it from seizure.

src.question: What is the expected course of a syncopal episode?
src.explanation: Syncope is by definition transient and self-limited, followed by spontaneous recovery, which is part of what separates it from seizure.

items.html: Cause of vasovagal syncope. The etiology is unclear, with a possible genetic predisposition, even though its triggers and reflex chain are well described.

src.question: What is known about the cause of vasovagal syncope?
src.explanation: The etiology of vasovagal syncope is unclear, with a possible genetic predisposition, even though its triggers and reflex chain are well described.

items.section_title: 2.1 · Definitions and the three syncope groups
items.html: Blood pressure and age. Normal values change with age, so a reading that is normal for an adult may be abnormal for an infant or child, and the reverse.

src.question: Why must a blood pressure reading be interpreted against the patient's age?
src.explanation: Blood pressure norms are affected by age, so a reading that is normal for an adult may be abnormal for an infant or child, and the reverse.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Orthostatic syncope: diagnosis and first-line care
items.html: First-line care for orthostatic syncope. Slow position changes limit the drop on standing, and treating the underlying cause addresses the diagnosis behind the hypotension.

src.question: Which measures are first-line for orthostatic syncope?
src.key: Slow position changes, treat the cause
src.explanation: Slow positional changes limit the drop on standing, and treating the underlying cause addresses the real diagnosis behind the hypotension.

items.html: Unavoidable vasovagal triggers. When a trigger cannot be avoided, such as blood draws, take safety precautions during the trigger, alongside trigger avoidance wherever possible.

src.question: A 30-year-old woman with vasovagal syncope must have regular blood draws for a chronic illness and has fainted at two of them. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
src.explanation: When a trigger cannot be avoided, safety precautions during the trigger are recommended, alongside trigger avoidance wherever possible.

items.section_title: 2.3 · Orthostatic syncope: diagnosis and first-line care
items.html: Orthostatic criterion with supine hypertension. With an elevated baseline or supine hypertension, the systolic fall must exceed 30 mmHg; a fall over 30 mmHg is needed.

src.question: A 72-year-old woman has supine hypertension (high blood pressure while lying flat). Lying down she is 176/96; after 3 minutes standing she is 152/90, and she feels mildly lightheaded. Do these readings meet the orthostatic criterion?
src.key: No; a fall over 30 mmHg is needed
src.explanation: With an elevated baseline or supine hypertension the systolic fall must exceed 30 mmHg; hers is 24 and the diastolic fall is only 6.

items.html: Heart rate criterion in adolescents. Adolescents need a heart rate increase of 40 beats per minute, whereas the adult threshold is 30.

src.question: A 15-year-old boy has lightheadedness on standing. Within 10 minutes his heart rate rises from 68 to 102, and his pressure is unchanged. Does this meet the heart rate criterion for his age?
src.key: No; adolescents need a rise of 40
src.explanation: His rise of 34 would exceed the adult threshold of 30, but in adolescents the threshold is an increase of 40 beats per minute.

items.html: Rheumatic mitral stenosis. It is rare in developed countries because rheumatic fever, its most common cause, has become less common there.

src.question: Why is rheumatic mitral stenosis rare in developed countries?
src.key: Rheumatic fever has become less common
src.explanation: Mitral stenosis is rare in developed countries because the incidence of rheumatic fever, its most common cause, has fallen there.

items.html: Tricuspid regurgitation neck findings. Raised jugular venous pressure with neck pulsations and a venous thrill over the right jugular vein, as blood is driven back into the right atrium.

src.question: Which neck findings fit tricuspid regurgitation?
src.key: Raised jugular pressure and a venous thrill
src.explanation: Tricuspid regurgitation raises the jugular venous pressure with neck pulsations and a venous thrill over the right jugular vein, as blood is driven back into the right atrium.

items.html: Chronic aortic regurgitation with reduced ejection fraction. With a mildly reduced or reduced ejection fraction, with or without symptoms, the next step is evaluation as a surgical candidate; untreated, survival is only about 2 to 3 years.

src.question: A 66-year-old man with chronic aortic regurgitation has no symptoms, but his echocardiogram now shows a reduced ejection fraction. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Chronic aortic regurgitation with a mildly reduced or reduced ejection fraction, with or without symptoms, makes the patient a surgical candidate. Left untreated, survival is only about 2 to 3 years.

items.html: Pulmonic regurgitation. It usually comes to attention as an incidental echo or exam finding, on echocardiogram or physical examination; the murmur is soft and hard to hear.

src.question: A 40-year-old woman with no cardiac symptoms is found to have pulmonic regurgitation. Which is the most common way this lesion comes to attention?
src.key: An incidental echo or exam finding
src.explanation: Pulmonic regurgitation is usually an incidental finding on an echocardiogram or on physical examination; the murmur is soft and hard to hear.

items.html: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome in adolescents. The heart rate threshold is an increase of 40 beats per minute within 10 minutes of standing; a rise exceeding 40 per minute meets it.

src.question: A 16-year-old girl has palpitations and dizziness on standing. Within 10 minutes of standing her heart rate rises from 70 to 114, and her pressure does not fall. Does this meet the heart rate criterion for her age?
src.key: Yes; the rise exceeds 40 per minute
src.explanation: In adolescents the threshold is an increase of 40 beats per minute; her rise of 44 within 10 minutes meets it.

items.section_title: 5.3 · Angina pectoris: the pain, silent ischemia and referred pain
items.html: Silent ischemia. Chest discomfort may be absent with diabetes, peripheral neuropathy and a transplanted heart; dyspnea, nausea and fatigue can be the presentation. Every chest pain workup starts with a stat electrocardiogram.

src.question: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has had two days of shortness of breath, nausea and fatigue, with no chest pain. Which is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: Chest discomfort may be absent in silent ischemia, which occurs with diabetes, peripheral neuropathy and a transplanted heart. Dyspnea, nausea and fatigue can be the presentation, and every chest pain workup starts with a stat electrocardiogram.

items.html: Suspected aortic dissection. A normal chest radiograph does NOT exclude dissection, so obtain immediate cross-sectional vascular imaging. Pain maximal at onset and asymmetric arm pressures point to it, and surgical involvement is urgent.

src.question: A 58-year-old hypertensive man has abrupt severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back, maximal at onset. His right arm pressure is 176/92 and his left is 138/78. A chest radiograph is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
src.explanation: A normal chest radiograph does NOT exclude dissection, so a normal film must not end the workup. The pain that is maximal at onset and the asymmetric arm pressures both point to it, and surgical involvement is urgent.
